messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 40

Dr. Meera Patel is an eighty-year-old South Asian woman who lives alone in a quiet apartment three blocks from the dental practice she ran for forty years. She still keeps the framed photograph of her graduation ceremony on the mantelpiece, beside a small bronze plaque that reads “Dr. M. Patel, BDS.” She retired five years ago, but her hands move with the same careful precision when she pours her morning tea—thumb and forefinger pinching the spout, a leftover habit from holding a mirror in a patient’s mouth.

That precision was not always a comfort.

The event happened fifty-two years ago, on a Saturday afternoon in Mumbai. Meera was thirty years old, newly married, and stepping out of a textile shop on Linking Road when a bomb concealed in a vegetable cart detonated fifty feet away. She remembers the pressure wave first—a wall of heat that slammed her backward through the shop’s glass door. Then the ringing, so high‑pitched it seemed to come from inside her skull. She remembers the dust: fine, grey, coating everything like a surgical mask that had been left out too long. Someone’s sandal landed near her hand. A child was screaming, a sharp wet sound, and Meera could not make her legs move. She lay on the shards of glass for what felt like minutes, watching a man stagger past with half his face gone, his teeth exposed in a way she would later recognize as a Le Fort III fracture—a dental detail her training forced her to register even then.

She was not physically injured beyond cuts and a ruptured eardrum. But for two years afterward she could not enter a shop without checking the exit first. She stopped going to markets. She insisted her husband drive her to work, and if he was late she would stand in the doorway with her keys clutched between her fingers like a dental explorer, ready to stab. Her hands began to shake during extractions. A colleague suggested she take a leave of absence; Meera refused, and instead began to wash her hands for three full minutes between every patient, counting the seconds in her head. The ritual gave her something to hold onto.

The marriage did not survive. Her husband called her cold, distant, too focused on control. She does not argue with that. She divorced him in her forties and raised her son alone. She told no one about the bomb. Not her son, not her patients. When she retired, she expected the memories to fade.

They did not.

Now, at eighty, Meera wakes most nights at 2:44 a.m.—the exact time she looked at her watch just before the blast—with her heart pounding so hard she can feel it in her temples. She lies still, listening for sirens that are not there. She keeps the bedroom light on because the dark makes her think of the dust cloud. She has not attended a Diwali celebration in thirty years because the firecrackers sound too much like the explosion. Yesterday, a delivery van backfired outside her building, and she dropped her teacup. She spent the next hour on her hands and knees, picking up every shard, lining them up by size on the kitchen counter—a dentist’s compulsion, she tells herself, though she knows it is something else.

Her son visits every Sunday. He brings her magazines and reminds her to call him if she feels “jumpy.” She says she is fine. She says old age is just noisy. But last week she found herself Googling the Mumbai blast of 1972 for the first time, reading the list of 37 dead and wondering if the man with the exposed teeth was among them. She closed the browser, washed her hands for three minutes, and then called her son to say she had a headache.

Meera does not tell him that sometimes, when she closes her eyes in the dental chair of her memory, she can still smell the cordite under the disinfectant. And she does not tell him that the only time she feels truly calm is when she folds her laundry—neat rectangles, aligned by color—because the repetition reminds her of the clean edges of a root canal, and because no one is bleeding.
